rain are used (BDB 564, 378, 973, 914). This is also a possible allusion to YHWH as the giver of fertility, not Ba'al

▣ "perfect" The Hebrew word (BDB 1071) means "self-sufficient," "whole," "complete" (cf. 2 Sam. 22:31; Ps. 18:30).

Notice the different ways YHWH is characterized (i.e. "the greatness of God," Deut. 32:3):

- His work is perfect ‒ BDB 1071

- all His ways are just ‒ BDB 1048

- a God of faithfulness ‒ BDB 53

- a God without injustice ‒ BDB 732

- He is righteous ‒ BDB 843

- He is upright ‒ BDB 449

What a powerful description of the God of creation and salvation. A God in whom all humans can trust
and rely (e.g. for other characterizations see Exod. 34:6; Num. 14:18; Deut. 4:31; Neh. 9:17; Ps. 103:8; 145:8).

▣ "A God of faithfulness" This is the same word (BDB 53) used in Deut. 32:20 referring to man's actions. It is
translated "faith" in Hab. 2:4, "the righteous will live by his faith." This shows the priority that God puts on His faithfulness
and Deut. 32:20 shows the priority He puts on the faith of His children. Faith and grace are both biblical concepts rather than
just NT concepts. The only way to respond to God's grace is through faith.

notes: The third person masculine singular שָׁחַת (shakhat) is rendered as third person masculine plural by Smr, a reading supported by the plural suffix on מוּם (mum, “defect”) as well as the plural of בֵּן (ben, “sons”).tn Heb “have acted corruptly” (so NASB, NIV84, NLT); NRSV “have dealt falsely.”
Heb “(they are) not his sons.”
Heb “defect” (so NASB). This highly elliptical line suggests that Israel’s major fault was its failure to act like God’s people; in fact, they acted quite the contrary.
Heb “twisted,” “crooked.” See Ps 18:26.

character (cf. Deut. 32:3-4), but did not, are described:

- "acted corruptly toward Him" ‒ BDB 1007, KB 1469, Piel PERFECT, cf. Deut. 4:16,25; 9:12;
31:29; Gen. 6:12; Exod. 32:7; described in Ps. 14:1-3, it usually denotes idolatry

- moral blemish, cf. Lev. 22:25; Job 11:15; Prov. 9:7

verses.zh: 愚昧无知的民哪，你们这样报答耶和华吗？他岂不是你的父、将你买来的吗？他是制造你、建立你的。
verses.en: Is this how you repay[NOTE:1] the Lord,you foolish, unwise people?Is he not your father, your Creator?He has made you and established you.
notes: Or “treat” (TEV).
verses.commentary:
32:6 "He your Father" The NIDOTTE, vol. 1, p. 222, has an interesting comment on this imagery for God. It is
used reluctantly in the OT because of the possible association with fertility worship (e.g. Jer. 2:27). This song of Moses
is one of the earliest usages to describe God (cf. Exod. 4:22; Deut. 1:31; 8:5 and later in the prophets, cf. Isa. 1:2; 63:16;
Jer. 3:19; Hosea 11:1-3; Mal. 1:6). YHWH's "fatherhood" is mentioned in Deut. 32:6,18 and 19-20.

This fatherhood of corporate Israel is identified in YHWH's relationship to the Davidic king (cf. 2 Sam. 7:14; Ps. 2:7; and 89:26).

Family imagery (father-son; husband-wife) is the most powerful ways to communicate the intimate
relationship that God desires with His human creation (made in His image and likeness, cf. Gen. 1:26-27). Humans can understand the
depth of God's feelings and commitment by analogy to these foundational human experiences (i.e. family, marriage, children).

verses.zh: 你当追想上古之日，思念历代之年；问你的父亲，他必指示你；问你的长者，他必告诉你。
verses.en: Remember the ancient days;bear in mind[NOTE:1] the years of past generations.[NOTE:2] Ask your father and he will inform you,your elders, and they will tell you.
notes: The Syriac, Targum, and Vulgate read second person masculine singular whereas the MT has second person masculine plural. The former is preferred, the latter perhaps being a misreading (בִּינוּ [binu] for בִּינָה [binah]). Both the preceding (“remember”) and following (“ask”) imperatives are singular forms in the Hebrew text.
Heb “generation and generation.” The repetition of the singular noun here singles out each of the successive past generations. See IBHS 116 §7.2.3b.
verses.commentary:
32:7 There are several commands in this verse related to Israel remembering YHWH's care and provision:

- "remember" ‒ BDB 269, KB 269, Qal IMPERATIVE

- "consider" ‒ BDB 106, KB 122, Qal IMPERATIVE

- "ask" ‒ BDB 981, KB 1371, Qal IMPERATIVE

- "elder will tell you" ‒ BDB 616, KB 665, Hiphil JUSSIVE

It was this historical information testified to in (1) the ancestral tradition passed down from generation
to generation (cf. Deut. 4:9-10; 6:7,20-25; 11:19; 32:46) and (2) this Song of Moses that witnessed against Israel!

verses.zh: 至高者将地业赐给列邦，将世人分开，就照以色列人的数目立定万民的疆界。
verses.en: When the Most High[NOTE:1] gave the nations their inheritance,when he divided up humankind,[NOTE:2] he set the boundaries of the peoples,according to the number of the heavenly assembly.[NOTE:3]
notes: The Hebrew term עֶלְיוֹן (ʿelyon) is an abbreviated form of the divine name El Elyon, frequently translated “God Most High” (so here NCV, CEV) or something similar. This full name (or epithet) occurs only in Gen 14, though the two elements are parallel in Pss 73:11; 107:11; etc. Here it is clear that Elyon has to do with the nations in general whereas in v. 9, by contrast, Yahweh relates specifically to Israel. See T. Fretheim, NIDOTTE 1:400-401. The title depicts God as the sovereign ruler of the world, who is enthroned high above his dominion.
Heb “the sons of man” (so NASB); or “the sons of Adam” (so KJV).

Heb “the sons of Israel.” The idea, perhaps, is that Israel was central to Yahweh’s purposes and all other nations were arranged and distributed according to how they related to Israel. See S. R. Driver, Deuteronomy (ICC), 355-56. For the MT בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל (bene yisraʾel, “sons of Israel”) a Qumran fragment has “sons of God,” while the LXX reads ἀγγέλων θεοῦ (angelōn theou, “angels of God”), presupposing בְּנֵי אֵל (bene ʾel) or בְּנֵי אֵלִים (bene ʾelim). “Sons of God” is undoubtedly the original reading; the MT and LXX have each interpreted it differently. MT assumes that the expression “sons of God” refers to Israel (cf. Hos. 1:10), while LXX has assumed that the phrase refers to the angelic heavenly assembly (Pss 29:1; 89:6; cf. as well Ps 82). The phrase is also attested in Ugaritic, where it refers to the high god El’s divine assembly. According to the latter view, which is reflected in the translation, the Lord delegated jurisdiction over the nations to his angelic host (cf. Dan. 10:13-21), while reserving for himself Israel, over whom he rules directly. For a defense of the view taken here, see M. S. Heiser, “Deuteronomy 32:8 and the Sons of God,” BSac 158 (2001): 52-74.
verses.commentary:
32:8 This verse asserts that Israel's God is also the only God (cf. Deut. 4:35,39; Isa. 54:5; Jer. 32:27). He and He alone
sets the boundaries of all nations (cf. Deut. 2:5,9,19; Genesis 10). This is not henotheism, but monotheism!

It is possible "the number of the sons of Israel" relates to the persons of Jacob's family who went into

verses.zh: 耶和华的分本是他的百姓；他的产业本是雅各。
verses.en: For the Lord’s allotment is his people,Jacob is his special possession.[NOTE:1]
notes: Heb “the portion of his inheritance.” The LXX and Smr add “Israel” and BHS suggests the reconstruction: “The Lord’s allotment is Jacob, the portion of his inheritance is Israel” (cf. NAB). While providing good parallelism, it destroys a fine chiastic structure: “allotment” (a), “his people” (b), “Jacob (b’), and “inheritance” (a’).
verses.commentary:
32:9 "the Lord's portion is His people" Conversely His people's portion is God
Himself (cf. Exod. 19:5; Ps. 16:5; 73:26; Lam. 3:24). The Israelites were in a unique sense YHWH's special covenant
people (cf. Deut. 4:20; 7:6; 14:2; 26:18).

verses.zh: 耶和华遇见他在旷野―荒凉野兽吼叫之地，就环绕他，看顾他，保护他，如同保护眼中的瞳人。
verses.en: The Lord[NOTE:1] found him[NOTE:2] in a desolate land,[NOTE:3]in an empty wasteland where animals howl.[NOTE:4] He continually guarded him[NOTE:5] and taught him;[NOTE:6] he continually protected him[NOTE:7] like the pupil[NOTE:8] of his eye.
notes: Heb “he.” The referent (the Lord) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

The reference is to “his people/Jacob” (cf. v. 9), that is, Israel (using a collective singular). The singular pronouns are replaced by plural ones throughout vv. 10-14 by some English versions as an aid to the modern reader (cf. NAB, NCV, TEV, NLT).

Heb “a land of wilderness.” A מִדְבָּר (midbar, “wilderness”) refers to a dry region which is characterized as receiving less than twelve inches of rain per year. It therefore cannot support trees and may or may not have sparse vegetation (if receiving less than six inches of rain). The point of the poetic image is that it is desolate.

Heb “in an empty, howling wasteland.” The word “howling” is derived from a verbal root that typically refers to the wailing of mourners. Here it likely refers to the howling of desert animals, or perhaps to the howling wind, in which case one may translate, “in an empty, windy wasteland.”

Heb “was surrounding him.” The distinctive form of the suffix on this verb form indicates that the verb is an imperfect, not a preterite. As such it draws attention to God’s continuing care during the period in view. See A. F. Rainey, “The Ancient Hebrew Prefix Conjugation in the Light of Amarnah Canaanite,” Hebrew Studies 27 (1986): 15-16.

Heb “he gave him understanding.” The form of the suffix on this verb form indicates that the verb is a preterite, not an imperfect. As such it simply states the action factually. See A. F. Rainey, “The Ancient Hebrew Prefix Conjugation in the Light of Amarnah Canaanite,” Hebrew Studies 27 (1986): 15-16.

The distinctive form of the suffix on this verb form indicates that the verb is an imperfect, not a preterite. As such it draws attention to God’s continuing protection during the period in view. See A. F. Rainey, “The Ancient Hebrew Prefix Conjugation in the Light of Amarnah Canaanite,” Hebrew Studies 27 (1986): 15-16.

Heb “the little man.” The term אִישׁוֹן (ʾishon) means literally “little man,” perhaps because when one looks into another’s eyes he sees himself reflected there in miniature. See A. Harman, NIDOTTE 1:391.

32:10 "He found him in a desert land,

And in the howling waste of a wilderness" This is an allusion to YHWH's choice of Israel in
romantic terms (cf. Jer. 2:23-; Hosea 2:14-15). This imagery supplements the exodus motif (cf. Deut. 1:19). It expresses in
powerful imagery YHWH's initiating love for Israel (cf. Deut. 10:14-15; Amos 3:2).

- Ezekiel 23

verses.zh: 又如鹰搅动巢窝，在雏鹰以上两翅搧展，接取雏鹰，背在两翼之上。
verses.en: Like an eagle that stirs up[NOTE:1] its nest,that hovers over its young,so the Lord[NOTE:2] spread out his wings and took him,[NOTE:3] he lifted him up on his pinions.
notes: The prefixed verbal form is an imperfect, indicating habitual or typical behavior. The parallel verb (cf. “hovers” in the next line) is used in the same manner.
Heb “he”; the referent (the Lord) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

The form of the suffix on this and the following verb forms (cf. “lifted him up”) indicates that the verbs are preterites, not imperfects. As such they simply state the action factually. The use of the preterite here suggests that the preceding verb (cf. “spread out”) is preterite as well.

verses.commentary:
32:13 "ride on the high places of the earth" This is imagery for

- YHWH's abundance (as is all of Deut. 32:14) given to Israel (cf. Isa. 58:14; Hab. 3:19)

- Israel's security (IVP Bible Background Commentary, p. 206)

▣ "he ate the produce of the field" This is what the MT has but the ancient versions saw that the context is about YHWH's
actions on Israel's behalf and changed the phrase to "He fed him with produce" (cf. LXX, Peshitta and Targums).

▣ "honey from the rock" This refers to the honey of wild bees, which often lived in the cracks of the rocks (cf. Ps. 81:16).

▣ "oil from the flinty rock" This refers to the wild olive trees that grew where not even grass could grow. Verses 13
and 14 are talking about the abundant produce of the Promised Land.

verses.zh: 但耶书仑渐渐肥胖，粗壮，光润，踢跳，奔跑，便离弃造他的　神，轻看救他的磐石；
verses.en: But Jeshurun[NOTE:1] became fat and kicked;you[NOTE:2] got fat, thick, and stuffed!Then he deserted the God who made him,and treated the Rock who saved him with contempt.
notes: To make the continuity of the referent clear, some English versions substitute “Jacob” here (NAB, NRSV) while others replace “Jeshurun” with “Israel” (NCV, CEV, NLT) or “the Lord’s people” (TEV).sn Jeshurun is a term of affection derived from the Hebrew verb יָשַׁר (yashar, “be upright”). Here it speaks of Israel “in an ideal situation, with its ‘uprightness’ due more to God’s help than his own efforts” (M. Mulder, TDOT 6:475).

The LXX reads the third person masculine singular (“he”) for the MT second person masculine singular (“you”), but such alterations are unnecessary in Hebrew poetic texts where subjects fluctuate frequently and without warning.
verses.commentary:
32:15-18 "fat" When Israel was blessed (cf. Deut. 31:20) she rejected YHWH:

- "forsook God (Eloah, cf. v. 17a) who made him" (cf. Deut. 32:6) ‒ BDB 643, KB 695, Qal IMPERFECT
with waw, cf. Deut. 31:16,17; Jdg. 10:6

- "scorned the Rock of his salvation" (cf. Deut. 32:4) ‒ BDB 614, KB 663, Piel IMPERFECT with waw, this
is the VERB form of the ADJECTIVE "foolish," found in Deut. 32:6 (cf. Ps. 74:18)

How did Israel "forsake" and "scorn" YHWH?

- they made Him jealous with strange gods, Deut. 32:16

- they made Him jealous with abominations, Deut. 32:16

- they sacrificed to demons, Deut. 32:17

- who were not known

IMPERFECT sense (only here)

forgetting the covenant is forgetting YHWH

Isa. 44:2). This is a touch of sarcasm (i.e. Deut. 32:15-16).

verses.zh: 耶和华看见他的儿女惹动他，就厌恶他们，说：
verses.en: But the Lord took note and despised thembecause his sons and daughters enraged him.
verses.commentary:
32:19-22 This paragraph is repetitious of preceding themes. Poetry is very repetitious. God's covenant people
reject Him and then He rejects them (cf. Hosea 1:9; 2:23; Rom. 9:25). His rejection (i.e. anger) is for the purpose of reconciliation. He
will use "a people" to provoke Israel to jealousy (and hopefully faith, cf. Rom. 11:11,14). This sounds very much to me like
Paul's discussion in Romans 9-11. Paul even quotes Deut. 32:21 in Rom. 10:19!

The added irony is that Israel left YHWH for non-existent gods (i.e. vanities, cf. Jer. 2:13). Oh, the
stupidity of human superstition and idolatry (cf. Isa. 40:19-20; 44:9-20; Jer. 10:3-5,14)!

32:19 The Dead Sea Scrolls (DSS) and Septuagint (LXX) add the phrase, "was jealous," which surely fits
the context but is absent in the Masoretic Text (MT).

verses.zh: 我要向他们掩面，看他们的结局如何。他们本是极乖僻的族类，心中无诚实的儿女。
verses.en: He said, “I will reject them.[NOTE:1] I will see what will happen to them;for they are a perverse generation,children[NOTE:2] who show no loyalty.
notes: Heb “I will hide my face from them.”
Heb “sons” (so NAB, NASB); TEV “unfaithful people.”
verses.commentary:
32:20 "I will hide My face from them" This is imagery for the cessation of YHWH's personal care and attention
(cf. Deut. 31:17-18).

SPECIAL TOPIC: GOD DESCRIBED AS HUMAN

▣ "I will see what their end shall be" YHWH had previously shown Moses the future of Israel in
Deut. 31:29, as He will later do for Joshua in Josh. 24:19.

▣ "For they are a perverse generation,

Sons in whom is no faithfulness" These two lines of poetry describe the tragedy of Israel who
had YHWH's special care and presence (cf. Rom. 9:4-5). They are characterized as:

- perverse (BDB 246) ‒ a term usually used in Proverbs (cf. Prov. 2:12,14; 6:14; 8:13; 10:31,31; 16:30; 23:33). It is
related to the Hebrew word for "stocks" (BDB 246), which put one's body into a crooked or twisted posture.

- no faithfulness (BDB 53 negated) ‒ a term also common to Proverbs (cf. Prov. 13:17; 20:6; also note Ps. 31:23;
Isa. 26:3; see SPECIAL TOPIC: BELIEVE,
TRUST, FAITH AND FAITHFULNESS IN THE OT).

- This characterization is parallel to Deut. 32:5:

- perverse (BDB 786 I)

- crooked (BDB 836)

YHWH is the true standard or rule (see SPECIAL TOPIC: RIGHTEOUSNESS). His covenant people have deviated from the standard.

verses.zh: 他们以那「不算为神」的触动我的愤恨，以虚无的神惹了我的怒气。我也要以那「不成子民」的触动他们的愤恨，以愚昧的国民惹了他们的怒气。
verses.en: They have made me jealous[NOTE:1] with false gods,[NOTE:2] enraging me with their worthless gods;[NOTE:3] so I will make them jealous with a people they do not recognize,[NOTE:4] with a nation slow to learn[NOTE:5] I will enrage them.
notes: They have made me jealous. The “jealousy” of God is not a spirit of pettiness prompted by his insecurity, but righteous indignation caused by the disloyalty of his people to his covenant grace (see note on the word “God” in Deut 4:24). The jealousy of Israel, however (see next line), will be envy because of God’s lavish attention to another nation. This is an ironic wordplay. See H. Peels, NIDOTTE 3:938-39.
Heb “what is not a god,” or a “nondeity.”

Heb “their empty (things).” The Hebrew term used here to refer pejoratively to the false gods is הֶבֶל (hevel, “futile” or “futility”), used frequently in Ecclesiastes (e.g., Eccl 1:1, “Futile! Futile!” laments the Teacher, “Absolutely futile! Everything is futile!”).
Heb “what is not a people,” or a “nonpeople.” The “nonpeople” (לֹא־עָם, loʾ ʿam) referred to here are Gentiles who someday would become God’s people in the fullest sense (cf. Hos 1:9; 2:23).
Heb “a foolish nation” (so KJV, NAB, NRSV); NIV “a nation that has no understanding”; NLT “I will provoke their fury by blessing the foolish Gentiles.”
verses.commentary:
32:21 "idols" This is literally "vapor" or "vanity" (BDB 210) and represents that which is worthless or
non-existent. Here, like Jer. 2:5; 8:19; 10:14-15; 16:19-20, it is used of idols. See a play on the word in Isa. 57:13.

SPECIAL TOPIC: IDOLATRY

SPECIAL TOPIC: MAGIC

verses.zh: 因为在我怒中有火烧起，直烧到极深的阴间，把地和地的出产尽都焚烧，山的根基也烧着了。
verses.en: For a fire has been kindled by my anger,and it burns to lowest Sheol;[NOTE:1] it consumes the earth and its produce,and ignites the foundations of the mountains.
notes: Sheol refers here not to hell and hell-fire—a much later concept—but to the innermost parts of the earth, as low down as one could get. The parallel with “the foundations of the mountains” makes this clear (cf. Pss 9:17; 16:10; 139:8; Isa 14:9, 15; Amos 9:2).tn Or “to the lowest depths of the earth”; cf. NAB “to the depths of the nether world”; NIV11 “to the realm of the dead below”; NLT “to the depths of the grave.”
verses.commentary:
32:22 This verse is imagery of the complete destruction and judgment that God will bring on rebellious
Israel (cf. Jer. 15:14; 17:4). All of God's creation (i.e. earth, sheol) are affected! This is not a reference to the
place of eternal punishment (see SPECIAL TOPIC: ETERNAL PUNISHMENT).

The imagery used in this verse is typical of the ANE view of creation. John H. Walton, ANE Thought
and the OT, describes this as "cosmic geology," see pp. 165-178. Also see John Walton, Genesis 1: An Ancient Cosmology.

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE DEAD, WHERE ARE THEY? (SHEOL/HADES, GEHENNA, TARTARUS), I., B.

▣ "the foundations of the mountains" The Hebrew Bible shares the ANE worldview of physical creation. Remember,
the ancient world is not anti-scientific, but pre-scientific (i.e. phenomenological language ‒ the descriptive language of the five senses).

- The earth's land is set on pillars (i.e. foundations) that come from the bottom of the seas (cf. 1 Sam. 2:8; Ps. 75:3; 104:5).

- Above the land is a dome shaped disk (see SPECIAL TOPIC: THE CIRCLE OF THE EARTH).

- YHWH did it! (Deut. 32:22; 1 Chr. 16:30; Job 38:4-6; Ps. 24:2; 102:25; Isa. 48:13; see SPECIAL TOPIC: THE AGE AND FORMATION OF THE EARTH)

For a good brief discussion of the ANE's worldview as illustrated from the OT, see John H. Walton, Ancient
Near Eastern Thought and the Old Testament: Introducing the Conceptual World of the Hebrew Bible, chapter 7, "Cosmic Geography," pp. 165-178; esp. pp. 174-175.

- consumed by plague, Deut. 32:24 (or famine, BDB 536 II, "burning heat")

verses.en: They will be starved by famine,eaten by plague, and bitterly stung;[NOTE:1] I will send the teeth of wild animals against them,along with the poison of creatures that crawl in the dust.
notes: The Hebrew term קֶטֶב (qetev) is probably metaphorical here for the sting of a disease (HALOT 1091-92 s.v.).

verses.zh: 外头有刀剑，内室有惊恐，使人丧亡，使少男、童女、吃奶的、白发的，尽都灭绝。
verses.en: The sword will make people childless outside,and terror will do so inside;they will destroy[NOTE:1] both the young man and the virgin,the infant and the gray-haired man.
notes: A verb is omitted here in the Hebrew text; for purposes of English style one suitable to the context is supplied.

verses.zh: 我说，我必将他们分散远方，使他们的名号从人间除灭。
verses.en: “I said, ‘I want to cut them in pieces.[NOTE:1] I want to make people forget they ever existed.
notes: The LXX reads “I said I would scatter them.” This reading is followed by a number of English versions (e.g., KJV, ASV, NIV, NCV, NRSV, NLT, CEV).
verses.commentary:
32:26-27 YHWH would have destroyed them:

- cut them to pieces, Deut. 32:26 ‒ BDB 802, KB 907, Hiphil IMPERFECT, but COHORTATIVE in
meaning to match the next VERB (only here, LXX has "scattered them"; NJB, "crush them to dust")

- remove the memory of them, Deut. 32:26 ‒ BDB 991, KB 1407, Hiphil COHORTATIVE (i.e. totally exterminate)

- This is only one of several texts which assert Israel's complete annihilation if they disobey the covenant (cf. Deut. 4:26; 28:20-22; 30:19).

But to do so would thwart His purpose for Israel. Israel's enemies would claim victory and attribute it to YHWH (cf. Deut. 32:27).

verses.zh: 惟恐仇敌惹动我，只怕敌人错看，说：是我们手的能力，并非耶和华所行的。
verses.en: But I fear the reaction[NOTE:1] of their enemies,for[NOTE:2] their adversaries would misunderstandand say, “Our power is great,[NOTE:3] and the Lord has not done all this!”’
notes: Heb “anger.”
Heb “lest.”

verses.commentary:
32:28-33 The question is to whom this paragraph is directed-Israel or their enemies (cf. Deut. 32:26-27)?

- Deut. 32:30 as reverse holy war

- Deut. 32:34-43 are about YHWH's rejection and judgment of Canaanite idolatry

32:28-29 Notice the words in Deut. 32:28-29 for "thinking":

- "no understanding in them" ‒ BDB 108 negated

- "that they were wise" ‒ BDB 314, KB 314, Qal PERFECT

Israel is incapable of right thinking!

verses.en: I wish that they were wise and could understand this,and that they could comprehend what will happen to them.”

verses.zh: 若不是他们的磐石卖了他们，若不是耶和华交出他们，一人焉能追赶他们千人？二人焉能使万人逃跑呢？
verses.en: How can one man chase a thousand of them,[NOTE:1] and two pursue ten thousand,unless their Rock had delivered them up[NOTE:2]—and the Lord had handed them over?
notes: The words “man” and “of them” are not in the Hebrew text, but are supplied in the translation for clarity.
Heb “sold them” (so NAB, NIV, NRSV, NLT).

32:30 Notice the parallel of verse 30 c and d:

- "their Rock had sold them" ‒ BDB 569, KB 581, Qal PERFECT, cf. Jdgs. 2:14; 3:8; 4:2; 10:7;
Ps. 44:10; Isa. 50:1

- "the Lord had given them up" ‒ BDB 688, KB 742, Hiphil PERFECT

Israel's defeat is possible because the divine Warrior (YHWH) has left them because of their covenant
disobedience. Verses 32-33 are imagery of wine symbolizing Canaanite worship. It is deadly (i.e. poison, bitter, venom)!

verses.zh: 据我们的仇敌自己断定，他们的磐石不如我们的磐石。
verses.en: For our enemies’[NOTE:1] rock is not like our Rock,as even our enemies concede.
notes: Heb “their,” but the referent (enemies) is specified in the translation for the sake of clarity.

verses.zh: 他们的葡萄树是所多玛的葡萄树，蛾摩拉田园所生的；他们的葡萄是毒葡萄，全挂都是苦的。
verses.en: For their vine is from the stock[NOTE:1] of Sodom,and from the fields of Gomorrah.[NOTE:2] Their grapes contain venom; their clusters of grapes are bitter.
notes: Heb “vine.”

Sodom…Gomorrah. The term “vine” is a reference to the pagan deities which, the passage says, find their ultimate source in Sodom and Gomorrah, that is, in the soil of perversion exemplified by these places (cf. Gen 18:20; 19:4-28; Isa 1:10; 3:9; Jer 23:14; Lam 4:6; Ezek 16:44-52; Matt 10:15; 11:23-24).

verses.zh: 他们的酒是大蛇的毒气，是虺蛇残害的恶毒。
verses.en: Their wine is snakes’ poison,the deadly venom of cobras.

verses.zh: 这不都是积蓄在我这里，封锁在我府库中吗？
verses.en: “Is this not stored up with me?” says the Lord,[NOTE:1] “Is it not sealed up in my storehouses?
notes: Verses 34-35 appear to be a quotation of the Lord and so the introductory phrase “says the Lord” is supplied in the translation.
verses.commentary:
32:34 It seems to me contextually that Deut. 32:34 can relate to Deut. 32:32-33. It is also possible that it
refers to Deut. 32:35 (a quote from YHWH [i.e. Deut. 32:34-35] like Deut. 32:39-42). The larger context is still YHWH
heaping judgment on Israel so that the nations will not get the wrong message. YHWH will judge them and vindicate
His people. It does not state whether Israel repents or that YHWH's eternal redemptive purposes must be allowed to
manifest in history. A rebellious covenant people is the lesser of two evils (i.e. the idolatrous nations). The Messiah
will come and Israel will still be covenant breakers!

This verse has two Qal PASSIVE PARTICIPLES:

- laid up in store ‒ BDB 485, KB 481 (found only here)

- sealed up ‒ BDB 367, KB 364, cf. Job 14:17

verses.zh: 他们失脚的时候，伸冤报应在我；因他们遭灾的日子近了；那要临在他们身上的必速速来到。
verses.en: I will get revenge and pay them backat the time their foot slips;for the day of their disaster is near,and the impending judgment[NOTE:1] is rushing upon them!”
notes: Heb “prepared things,” “impending things.” See BDB 800 s.v. עָתִיד.
verses.commentary:
32:35 The first line of this verse is quoted in the NT in Rom. 12:19 and Heb. 10:30. The term "vengeance"
(BDB 668) is also mentioned in Deut. 32:41 and 43. It is often used by Isaiah and Jeremiah:

- against Israel ‒ Isa. 59:17

- against Israel's enemies ‒ Isa. 34:8; 35:4; 61:2; 63:4; Jer. 46:10; 50:15,18; 51:6,11

The term "retribution" (BDB 1024) is also found in Isa. 59:18 (twice) in a context where YHWH will
restore a sinful Israel (i.e. Zion).

▣ "In due time their foot will slip" This VERB (BDB 556, KB 555, Qal IMPERFECT) can refer to:

- a personal fall into trouble ‒ David in Ps. 38:17

- a divine judgment ‒ Isa. 24:19

- a divine promise of restoration ‒ Ps. 94:18; Isa. 54:10

Humans stumble and nature is disrupted (cf. Isa. 24:19), but YHWH will restore both (cf. Rom. 8:18-25).

▣ The last two lines of poetry in Deut. 32:35 denote the rapid and sure coming of YHWH's justice:

- day of calamity (BDB 15) is near (BDB 898)

- the impending things are hastening upon them (BDB 301 I, KB 300, Qal ACTIVE PARTICIPLE)

verses.zh: 耶和华见他百姓毫无能力，无论困住的、自由的都没有剩下，就必为他们伸冤，为他的仆人后悔。
verses.en: The Lord will judge his people,and will change his plans concerning[NOTE:1] his servants;when he sees that their power has disappeared,and that no one is left, whether confined or set free.
notes: The translation understands the verb in the sense of “be grieved, relent” (cf. HALOT 689 s.v. נחם hitp 2); cf. KJV, ASV “repent himself”; NLT “will change his mind”; NIV11 “relent.” Another option is to translate “will show compassion to” (see BDB 637 s.v. נחם); cf. NASB, NIV84, NRSV.
verses.commentary:
32:36 In this song of warning and prediction of Israel's disobedience resulting in divine judgment, there is
also the promise of YHWH's forgiveness and restoration.

- The Lord will vindicate His people ‒ BDB 192, KB 220, Qal IMPERFECT, cf. Ps. 135:14

- The Lord will have compassion on His servants ‒ BDB 636, KB 688, Hithpael
IMPERFECT

YHWH will judge His people (Ps. 7:8; 96:10), but in so doing, will establish them!

verses.commentary:
32:39-40 YHWH establishes His uniqueness. There is no pantheon! Notice the use of antithetical parallelism:

- See ‒ BDB 906, KB 1157, Qal IMPERATIVE

- I am He ‒ cf. Exod. 3:13-14 (YHWH; see SPECIAL TOPIC: NAMES FOR DEITY, D.)

- I have wounded, and it is I who heal ‒ cf. Job 5:18; Isa. 45:7; Hosea 6:1; Amos 3:6 (often in the OT all causality is
attributed to God as a way to express the truth of monotheism)

- There is no one who can deliver from My hand ‒ cf. Ps. 50:22; Isa. 43:13; Dan. 4:35

In Deut. 32:40 YHWH (the ever-living, only living God) takes an oath by His own character! This lifting of

verses.zh: 我若磨我闪亮的刀，手掌审判之权，就必报复我的敌人，报应恨我的人。
verses.en: I will sharpen my lightning-like sword,and my hand will grasp hold of the weapon of judgment;[NOTE:1] I will execute vengeance on my foes,and repay those who hate me![NOTE:2]
notes: Heb “judgment.” This is a metonymy, a figure of speech in which the effect (judgment) is employed as an instrument (sword, spear, or the like), the means, by which it is brought about.

The Hebrew term שָׂנֵא (saneʾ, “hate”) in this covenant context speaks of those who reject Yahweh’s covenant overtures, that is, who disobey its stipulations (see note on the word “rejecting” in Deut 5:9; also see Deut 7:10; 2 Chr 19:2; Pss 81:15; 139:20-21).
verses.commentary:
32:41-43 YHWH describes His actions of justice against idolaters (Deut. 32:41-42). In Deut. 32:43 He asserts His
commitment to Israel.

Paul uses the first line of Deut. 32:43 in Rom. 15:10 and asserts that it shows that YHWH loves and
includes Gentiles. Paul, in Romans 15, also quotes Ps. 18:49 or 2 Sam. 22:5; Ps. 117:1 and Isa. 11:10; 42:4 (cf. Matt. 12:21)
to assert the same truth.

YHWH is willing to forgive Israel based on His character and promises, not their actions. This, in essence, is
the new covenant of Jer. 31:31-34 and Ezek. 36:22-36. Human hope is ultimately in the unchanging character of a gracious
God in Whose image and likeness they are created!

verses.commentary:
32:43 "Rejoice" This VERB (BDB 943, KB 1247) is a Qal IMPERATIVE. It is a
shout of joy, cf. Job 38:7; Isa. 12:6; 24:14; 44:23; 49:13; 54:1; Jer. 31:7. But, who is to rejoice and for what reason?

The Jewish Study bible, p. 444, asserts that v. 43, as it stands in the MT, cannot be right.

- "rejoice you nations who are being judged" does not make sense

- the parallelism between the first two lines is unclear (unless the "gods" is paralled with "nations," cf. Deut. 32:8)

- v. 43 has many problems in the MT

- the LXX and DSS have a different version that makes more sense

"Rejoice, O believers with Him!

Worship Him, O every one!

For He'll avenge the blood of His children

Wreak vengeance on His foes;

He will repay those who hate Him,

And cleanse the land of His people."

The UBS Text Project, p. 305-307, supports this rendering with a "B" rating (some doubt). This is the
translation of the NEB, REB, NRSV.

The DSS and LXX add a phrase after line 1, "and let all the angels of God prevail for him." The NRSV translates
this as, "worship him, all you gods," and REB, "bow down all you gods, before him."

The DSS and LXX also add a phrase after line 3, "and he will repay those who hate" (see NRSV, REB, NJB).

Joshua is positioned with Moses before the people to confirm and establish his leadership role.

says he died and was buried at Moseroth (cf. Num. 33:30-31). Hard Sayings of the Bible, p. 166, says Moserah is the
name of the area and Mount Hor (BDB 246) the name of the specific mountain.

READING CYCLE THREE (see "Bible Interpretation Seminar")

FOLLOWING THE ORIGINAL AUTHOR'S INTENT AT PARAGRAPH LEVEL

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible.
Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare your subject divisions with the five translations above. Paragraphing
is not inspired, but it is the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every paragraph has one and only one subject.

CONTEXTUAL INSIGHTS

- This may be a specific type of literary genre of the ANE whereby a leader gives his last blessing, warning,
and prophecy before his death:

- Jacob ‒ Genesis 49 (also poetic form)

- Moses ‒ Deut. 29:2-34:12

- Joshua ‒ Josh. 23:1-24:33

- Samuel ‒ 1 Samuel 12

- David ‒ 1 Kgs. 2:1-9

- Some scholars see this poem: (1) in light of a Hittite treaty pattern, but (2) others see it as a court scene. In the
context of the book of Deuteronomy, option 2 seems best, although the whole book of Deuteronomy fits the
second millennium B.C. treaty pattern (which gives evidence for Mosaic authorship). See VII,
Introduction to Deuteronomy.

SPECIAL TOPIC: HITTITE (Suzerain) TREATIES

- The poem is ancient (archaic forms). Almost all scholars assume it goes back to ancient times in Israel's history.

- There are many allusions to songs in the OT, particularly Psalms and Isaiah. They are sung at times of victory:

- the Egyptian palace guard destroyed in the Red Sea, Exodus 15

- before Israel enterred the transJordan, Num. 21:17

- the Canaanite army of Hazor destroyed, Judges 5

- Babylon destroyed (Isaiah 13) by YHWH's Messiah (Isaiah 11), Isa. 12:5

- SPECIAL TOPIC: HEBREW POETRY
